clue.text: Entertainment for the sweet-toothed?

parts.note: Graham Greene labelled some of his thrillers 'entertainments', and one of them shares its name with a hard seaside stick of sugar candy

explanation.surface: A question about what treat would amuse someone with a sweet tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: Greene sorted his books into novels and 'entertainments'; this 1938 one is named after the striped candy sold at a south-coast English resort, so it entertains the sweet-toothed twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greene thriller is one of his self-styled entertainments and is titled after a sugary seaside confection.

clue.text: "Nature's gives nothing, but doth lend" (Shakespeare)

parts.note: a line from Shakespeare's fourth sonnet with one word missing after 'Nature's'; the gap is a legacy left by will

explanation.surface: A quotation from a sonnet with a word left out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: Sonnet 4 reads 'Nature's ___ gives nothing but doth lend': the missing noun means something handed down in a will, contrasted with a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: The word missing from the sonnet line is a legacy, set against lending.

clue.text: Tarkington finally offered Josephine's

parts.note: Booth Tarkington's last novel was titled 'The ___ of Josephine'; the missing word is a likeness or representation

explanation.surface: A remark about what the novelist Tarkington ended up offering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' is not a last-letter signal here: Tarkington's final novel (1945) was The Image of Josephine, so the clue is a title with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in the title of Tarkington's last book is a word for a likeness or picture.

clue.text: Shakespearean suitor morphs into horse

indicators.note: to morph is to change shape, so the letters of the following words are reshaped

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare character turns into a horse, as in a fairy-tale transformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'morphs' rearranges INTO HORSE. The suitor is Bianca's wooer in The Taming of the Shrew.
explanation.definitionFit: He courts Bianca, disguised as a music teacher, in The Taming of the Shrew.

clue.text: Lubricates art

explanation.surface: A curt instruction about greasing the wheels of art.
explanation.definitionFit: To lubricate is to grease with liquid fat, and oil paintings are works of art.

clue.text: "Walter ordered a broiled fish and a bottle of" (Patricia Highsmith, The Blunderer)

definitions.text: "Walter ordered a broiled fish and a bottle of" (Patricia Highsmith, The Blunderer)

parts.words: "Walter ordered a broiled fish and a bottle of" (Patricia Highsmith, The Blunderer)
parts.note: a sentence from Highsmith's novel with the last word missing; what goes with fish is a white wine from the Rhine and Mosel

explanation.surface: A quoted line from a Highsmith novel about a man ordering dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a dry white German grape wine, a classic match for fish.

clue.text: Firbank's whim places church on this island

indicators.note: the clue says church placed on the island gives Firbank's book, so the church abbreviation is taken back off that title

parts.note: Ronald Firbank wrote the novel Caprice; a caprice is a whim
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A novelist's fancy puts a church on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards from the surface: 'places church on this island' means island + CE = CAPRICE, Firbank's 1917 novel, so removing CE leaves the island in the Bay of Naples.
explanation.definitionFit: The island in the Bay of Naples is the one the clue points at as 'this'.

clue.text: Bold harp composition from Windsor tapster

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tavern servant from Windsor composes a piece for a bold harp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' rearranges BOLD HARP. In The Merry Wives of Windsor Falstaff's follower is taken on as tapster at the Garter Inn.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff's red-nosed follower becomes a drawer of ale at the Garter in The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: Composer in firm following directions

parts.note: E, N, E and S are compass points
CO is short for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A musician employed by a company that follows instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts CO (firm) after the compass points ENES. The composer is the Romanian George Enescu, often written Enesco.
explanation.definitionFit: George Enescu, Romanian violinist and author of the Romanian Rhapsodies, is often spelt Enesco in English.

clue.text: Dance play

explanation.surface: Two words pairing a dance with a play, as on a theatre bill.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a square dance for four couples, and also a Noel Coward play of 1952.

clue.text: Simple as the pleasures of Bowles ()

explanation.surface: Something called simple, like the pleasures a writer named Bowles described.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Bowles's story collection is Plain Pleasures; the empty brackets stand where the letter count would be.
explanation.definitionFit: Simple means unadorned, and Jane Bowles titled her story collection after unadorned pleasures.

clue.text: Henry's uncle of Hardy's Exonbury

explanation.surface: A royal relative linked to a town in Thomas Hardy's Wessex.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry V the Duke of this title is the king's uncle; Hardy's fictional Wessex renames the Devon cathedral city Exonbury.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke so titled is Henry V's uncle in Shakespeare, and Hardy disguised the Devon county town as Exonbury.

clue.text: Atlas issue

parts.note: not an edition of a map book: the offspring of the Titan Atlas, seven sisters who became a star cluster

explanation.surface: An edition of a book of maps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Atlas' looks like the map book and 'issue' like an edition; issue means children, and Atlas's seven daughters became the star cluster in Taurus.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione were set in the sky as a star cluster.

clue.text: Bennett's girl of the Roman road

definitions.text: Bennett's girl of the Roman road

parts.words: Bennett's girl of the Roman road
parts.note: Arnold Bennett wrote the novel '... of Watling Street', and Watling Street is a Roman road across England

explanation.surface: A novelist's heroine from an ancient Roman highway.
explanation.walkthrough: Watling Street is a Roman road running from Kent to the Midlands; Bennett's 1904 novel names its heroine after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett titled a 1904 novel after this woman, naming her by Watling Street.

clue.text: Storytelling uncle perhaps

explanation.surface: An uncle who likes to tell stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A narration of events is a telling, and an uncle is one example of a kinsman.

clue.text: With which to make an incisive design statement

definitions.text: With which to make an incisive design statement

parts.words: With which to make an incisive design statement
parts.note: incisive is meant literally: a design cut into the surface of a gem or metal, the reverse of a cameo

explanation.surface: Advice on how to make a sharp, bold mark in design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incisive' reads as sharp or bold, but here it means cut in: the craft engraves a sunken design into stone or metal.
explanation.definitionFit: This carving technique cuts a sunken figure into the surface, as on a seal.

clue.text: Subject matter for Allen and Besant

definitions.text: Subject matter for Allen and Besant

parts.words: Subject matter for Allen and Besant
parts.note: Walter Besant wrote 'The ... Box', and Grant Allen also took the same pale carving stone as a title

explanation.surface: What two Victorian writers chose to write about.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine white carving stone named a box in Besant's title and furnished a title for Allen too.

clue.text: His autobiography reveals a perfect stranger

definitions.text: His autobiography reveals a perfect stranger

parts.words: His autobiography reveals a perfect stranger
parts.note: the poet P. J. ... titled his 1966 memoir 'The Perfect Stranger'

explanation.surface: A man's memoir shows him to be someone nobody knew.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a revealing confession; in fact The Perfect Stranger is the title of P. J. Kavanagh's memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: P. J. Kavanagh, English poet, wrote the memoir The Perfect Stranger.

clue.text: Let in some sort of light for Woolf character

indicators.note: the word for let is placed inside the word for the light

parts.note: daylight is a sort of light, giving DAY
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: Admit a kind of light for a character in a Virginia Woolf novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts ALLOW (let) inside DAY, the 'day' of daylight. Clarissa is the heroine of Woolf's Mrs Dalloway.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarissa, the society hostess of Woolf's 1925 novel, bears this surname.

clue.text: On several occasions he wrote poems

definitions.text: On several occasions he wrote poems

parts.words: On several occasions he wrote poems
parts.note: 'Poems on Several Occasions' is a classic title for such books

explanation.surface: A remark that someone wrote poetry now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On several occasions' seems to mean now and then, but it echoes the old title form 'Poems on Several Occasions', apt for Austin Dobson, writer of occasional verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Austin Dobson was a Victorian writer of polished light and occasional verse.

clue.text: Quiet musketeer engages sympathy

parts.note: p (piano) is the musical mark for quiet
Athos is one of Dumas's three musketeers

explanation.surface: A silent swordsman wins someone's sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet. Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers.
explanation.definitionFit: A quality that moves to pity, close to sympathy in sense.

clue.text: Second journalist on the French Connection

parts.note: a hack is a slang word for a journalist
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: A reporter follows up on the film The French Connection.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invokes the film The French Connection; the definition is just 'Connection', a fetter or link.
explanation.definitionFit: A fetter or tie, something that binds and so connects.

clue.text: Wager your chap heard poet

parts.note: to wager is to bet

indicators.note: the clue words are to be taken as spoken, so their sound gives the letters

parts.note: said casually, your man comes out as 'yer man'

explanation.surface: A gambler bets on a man he has heard reciting poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' makes 'yer man' (your chap, said casually) the sound of the poet's -jeman ending, after BET (wager).
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Betjeman was Poet Laureate from 1972.

clue.text: Macabre artist measures alternative

parts.note: ens are printers' measures of width
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A painter of grim subjects measures up an alternative.
explanation.walkthrough: An en is a printers' unit of width, half an em. James Ensor was a Belgian painter of masks and skeletons.
explanation.definitionFit: James Ensor, Belgian painter, filled his canvases with skeletons and grotesque masks.

clue.text: Spanish novelist gets German agreement to follow wild boar

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of boar run riot into a new order

parts.note: ja is German for yes

explanation.surface: A Spanish writer gets a German's agreement to go after a wild boar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges BOAR into BARO; JA (German yes) follows it, signalled by 'to follow'. Pio Baroja was a Basque novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Pio Baroja, Basque writer of the Generation of '98, is a leading Spanish novelist.

clue.text: How Cicero would speak (at zero speed) ()

parts.note: o looks like the figure zero
rate is a speed

explanation.surface: A question of how the Roman orator would talk at a standstill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at zero speed' looks like a comment on Cicero's slow delivery; it gives O + RATE. The empty brackets stand where the count would be.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero was the great Roman orator, so speaking like him is making a formal speech.

clue.text: Many support poet in his work

indicators.note: in a down answer the supporting piece sits beneath the piece it holds up

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe is the American poet
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, many

explanation.surface: Many people back a poet in his writing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'support' puts M (Roman thousand) under POE. 'his work' then refers back to the poet: a poem is what a poet writes.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of verse is the work a poet produces.

clue.text: Former pupils take Old English woodwinds ()

indicators.note: the word for former pupils takes in, or holds, the abbreviation

parts.note: OBs are old boys, former pupils of a school

explanation.surface: Old boys of a school learn Old English and play wind instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' puts OE (Old English) inside OBS (old boys). The empty brackets stand where the count would be.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-reed instruments of the woodwind section.

clue.text: P. H. Newby found many from whom to enquire

definitions.text: P. H. Newby found many from whom to enquire

parts.words: P. H. Newby found many from whom to enquire
parts.note: P. H. Newby's last novel bears a title meaning an excessive demand, which can also be read as plenty of people to question

explanation.surface: A novelist discovered plenty of people to put his questions to.
explanation.walkthrough: Newby's 1991 novel title is an idiom for an unreasonable request; read literally it means a great number of people to ask, which the clue's 'many from whom to enquire' spells out.
explanation.definitionFit: P. H. Newby's final novel is titled with the idiom for an unreasonable demand.

clue.text: English writer — German rage he stirs up

indicators.note: stirring up mixes contents around, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A German's anger is roused, and he stirs things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirs up' rearranges GERMAN RAGE HE. He also wrote the 1-across novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Greene was the English novelist of The Power and the Glory and The Third Man.
